lead: This unit shows how a system's output moves in time after a sudden input. By the end you can name the standard inputs, read order and type from a transfer function, sketch first- and second-order responses from τ, ζ and ωn, compute the five time-domain specifications, and find the steady-state error with static or dynamic error constants.
about: Time response analysis answers one question: when the input changes, how does the output get to its final value, and how far off is it at the end? Chapter 2.1 defines the four standard inputs every later result is measured against. Chapter 2.2 separates order (how many poles) from type (how many poles sit at the origin). Chapter 2.3 takes a single pole and finds the one time constant that fixes everything. Chapter 2.4 adds a second pole and the damping ratio, giving four possible shapes. Chapter 2.5 turns those shapes into five numbers an exam can ask for. Chapter 2.6 finds the error left after the transient dies, using Kp, Kv and Ka. Chapter 2.7, taught by only a few universities, replaces those constants with a series for inputs that are not pure steps or ramps.

chapters.idea: Four ideal inputs — impulse, step, ramp and parabola — stand in for every real command, so that responses can be compared like for like.
chapters.depth: Define each signal in the time domain and give its Laplace transform: δ(t) → 1, 1(t) → 1/s, t·1(t) → 1/s², (t²/2)·1(t) → 1/s³. Draw all four. State the relations: step is the integral of the impulse, ramp is the integral of the step, parabola is the integral of the ramp, and the reverse by differentiation. Give the sifting property of the impulse, ∫f(t)δ(t−a)dt = f(a). Give the physical source of each: step = switch closed or valve opened, ramp = antenna tracking a satellite or a target moving at constant speed, parabola = a target accelerating, impulse = a hammer blow or a very short pulse. Explain scaling: r(t) = A·1(t) has R(s) = A/s. Some syllabi call this chapter 'standard test inputs' or 'standard test signals and their importance'.

figure.aria: A graph with time on the horizontal axis showing the unit step sitting at 1, the unit ramp rising as a straight line, and the unit parabolic input rising as t squared by two.

chapters.example: A command is r(t) = 2·1(t) + 3t·1(t) − 2δ(t), where 1(t) is the unit step and δ(t) the unit impulse. Find R(s). Answer: R(s) = 2/s + 3/s² − 2. The constant 2 gives 2/s, the ramp of slope 3 gives 3/s², and the impulse of strength 2 gives 2, because L{δ(t)} = 1.
chapters.trap: The unit parabolic input is t²/2, not t². Writing 1/s² for a parabola, or leaving out the factor 1/2, loses marks in almost every paper.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: transfer function and Laplace transform of standard functions.
chapters.leave: Laplace transform properties and partial fractions to the mathematics course; the full error analysis to Chapters 2.6 and 2.7.

chapters.idea: Order is the number of poles of the open-loop transfer function; type is how many of those poles sit at the origin — type fixes the steady-state error, order fixes the shape of the transient.
chapters.depth: Write the open-loop transfer function in pole-zero form, G(s) = K·(s+z₁)(s+z₂)… / [s^N·(s+p₁)(s+p₂)…]. Order n = degree of the denominator after cancelling common factors. Type N = number of poles at s = 0. Work through type 0, 1, 2 and 3 examples. Show the time-constant form, G(s) = K'·(1+sT₁)(1+sT₂)… / [s^N·(1+sT_a)(1+sT_b)…], and show how K and K' differ by the product of the zero and pole magnitudes. State clearly that type and order describe the open-loop transfer function of a unity feedback system; for non-unity feedback, first reduce to an equivalent unity feedback open-loop form. Note that some syllabi use 'system type' or 'error type' for N.

figure.aria: A tree splitting the open-loop transfer function 5(s+2)/s squared (s+3)(s+4) into order 4 from the denominator degree and type 2 from the two poles at the origin.

chapters.example: For G(s) = 20(s+3)/[s²(s+1)(s+5)] find the order, the type, and the time-constant form. Answer: the denominator has degree 2 + 1 + 1 = 4, so order = 4. There are two poles at s = 0, so type = 2. Time-constant form: pull the constants out, 20 × 3 / (1 × 5) = 12, giving G(s) = 12(1 + s/3) / [s²(1 + s)(1 + s/5)] = 12(1 + 0.333s)/[s²(1 + s)(1 + 0.2s)].
chapters.trap: Zeros do not change order, and poles not at the origin do not change type. A common error is counting all poles for type, or treating a pole at s = −0.001 as if it were at the origin.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: transfer function; Chapter 2.1 for the inputs used later with each type.
chapters.leave: Block diagram reduction and signal flow graphs to Unit 1; pole locations and stability to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A first-order system has one time constant τ, and τ alone decides how fast the output moves: 63.2% of the final value at t = τ, about 95% at 3τ, about 98% at 4τ.
chapters.depth: Standard form G(s) = K/(1+τs), with a pole at s = −1/τ; the alternative form K/(s+a) with a = 1/τ. Derive the step response c(t) = K(1 − e^(−t/τ)) by partial fractions; mark the initial slope K/τ and the 63.2% point. Derive the ramp response c(t) = K(t − τ + τe^(−t/τ)) and show the steady-state lag of τ seconds. Derive the impulse response c(t) = (K/τ)e^(−t/τ). Derive the parabolic response and show the steady-state error grows with t. State that moving the pole left (smaller τ) makes the system faster and moving it right makes it slower. Note that the closed-loop first-order system with unity feedback also has one time constant, τ/(1+K). Some syllabi call the step response the 'transient response' and the τ-based curve the 'exponential response'.

figure.aria: A graph of the first-order step response rising to 1 within four time constants, next to the ramp response that settles into a straight line parallel to the input and lagging by one time constant.

chapters.example: A first-order system has G(s) = 10/(1 + 2s) and is given a unit step at t = 0. (a) Write c(t). (b) Find the time to reach 9, that is 90% of the final value 10. (c) Give the steady-state output for a unit ramp. Answer: here K = 10 and τ = 2 s, so c(t) = 10(1 − e^(−t/2)). For 9 = 10(1 − e^(−t/2)) we get e^(−t/2) = 0.1, so t = 2 ln 10 = 4.605 s. For a unit ramp the steady state is 10(t − 2), a line of slope 10 lagging the scaled input by τ = 2 s.
chapters.trap: τ is not the settling time. Reaching 98% takes 4τ, and 5τ is only an engineering rule of thumb. Also do not drop K: the final value is K, not 1, when the system has gain.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for the inputs; Chapter 2.2 for order and type.
chapters.leave: Steady-state error constants to Chapter 2.6; higher-order systems and dominant poles to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A second-order system has two numbers, ωn for speed and ζ for shape; ζ sorts the response into undamped, underdamped, critically damped and overdamped.
chapters.depth: Standard form G(s) = ωn²/(s² + 2ζωn s + ωn²), with poles s = −ζωn ± jωn√(1−ζ²). Define ζ (damping ratio, unitless) and ωn (undamped natural frequency, rad/s). Classify: ζ = 0 undamped, 0 < ζ < 1 underdamped, ζ = 1 critically damped, ζ > 1 overdamped. Derive the step response for each case by partial fractions. For the underdamped case use ωd = ωn√(1−ζ²) (damped frequency) and φ = cos⁻¹ζ, giving c(t) = 1 − (1/√(1−ζ²))e^(−ζωn t)·sin(ωd t + φ) for unity DC gain. Give the critically damped form c(t) = 1 − (1 + ωn t)e^(−ωn t). Give the overdamped form with two real roots s₁, s₂. Sketch all four on one set of axes. Show that changing ζ moves the poles along a circle of radius ωn, and changing ωn scales the circle — this is the 'effect of moving the pole in the s-plane'. Mention in one line that an added real pole or zero bends the response, and that only a few universities examine that here.

figure.aria: A graph of four second-order step responses with the same natural frequency, showing sustained oscillation at damping ratio zero, large overshoot at 0.3, no overshoot at 1, and a slow crawl at 2.

chapters.example: For G(s) = 25/(s² + 6s + 25) find ζ, ωn, ωd, the peak overshoot and the peak time. Answer: compare with s² + 2ζωn s + ωn², so ωn² = 25 giving ωn = 5 rad/s, and 2ζωn = 6 giving ζ = 6/(2 × 5) = 0.6, so the system is underdamped. ωd = 5√(1 − 0.36) = 5 × 0.8 = 4 rad/s. Peak overshoot Mp = e^(−πζ/√(1−ζ²)) = e^(−π × 0.6/0.8) = e^(−2.356) = 0.0948, that is 9.48%. Peak time tp = π/ωd = π/4 = 0.785 s.
chapters.trap: Getting ζ wrong by forgetting the 2: the coefficient of s is 2ζωn, not ζωn. Also the overshoot formula takes the angle in radians inside the exponential, and √(1−ζ²) must be real, so check ζ < 1 before using the underdamped formulas.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for the step input; Chapter 2.2 for the standard second-order form; school-level quadratic roots and trigonometry.
chapters.leave: Stability from pole position and Routh-Hurwitz to Unit 3; M circles and Nichols chart to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Five numbers — delay time, rise time, peak time, peak overshoot and settling time — squeeze the whole transient into a short specification sheet.
chapters.depth: Define each specification precisely, with the measurement condition. Delay time td: time to reach 50% of the final value; give the approximation td ≈ (1 + 0.7ζ)/ωn. Rise time tr: for the 0–100% definition tr = (π − φ)/ωd with φ = cos⁻¹ζ; note that the 10–90% definition gives a different number and say which one is being used. Peak time tp = π/ωd. Peak overshoot Mp = e^(−πζ/√(1−ζ²)), often given as a percentage. Settling time ts: the envelope e^(−ζωn t)/√(1−ζ²) stays inside a band, giving ts ≈ 4/(ζωn) for a 2% band and ts ≈ 3/(ζωn) for a 5% band. Show each quantity on a marked sketch. State the assumptions: standard second-order transfer function, unity DC gain, no zeros, and formulas are approximations. Also show the reverse problem: from given Mp and ts, find ζ and ωn.

figure.aria: A graph of the underdamped step response for damping ratio 0.5 with two flat lines at 1.02 and 0.98, showing the output entering the two per cent band for the last time near eight seconds.

chapters.trap: Mixing the rise-time definitions, and applying these formulas to a transfer function that has a zero or a gain other than 1. The formulas describe the standard second-order form only.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.4 for ζ, ωn, ωd and φ.
chapters.leave: Improving these numbers with a controller or compensator to Unit 5; the frequency-domain version of the same specifications to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: After the transient dies, the error that remains depends only on the system type and the input type, and three static error constants give it in one line.
chapters.depth: Start from E(s) = R(s)/(1 + G(s)) for unity negative feedback, where G(s) is the open-loop transfer function. Apply the final value theorem, ess = lim s→0 sE(s), and state its condition: all closed-loop poles must lie in the left half plane (link to Unit 3). Define the static error constants: position Kp = lim s→0 G(s), velocity Kv = lim s→0 sG(s), acceleration Ka = lim s→0 s²G(s). Give ess = 1/(1+Kp) for a unit step, 1/Kv for a unit ramp, 1/Ka for a unit parabola, and state that a constant A scales the input and the error. Build the type-versus-input table for type 0, 1, 2 and 3: finite, zero or infinite in each cell. Explain the trade-off: adding an integrator (raising the type) reduces error but pushes the system towards instability. Mention non-unity feedback briefly: the error at the comparator is E = R − H·C, so use 1/(1 + GH). Some syllabi call these 'static error coefficients'; the values Kp, Kv, Ka are also called 'error constants'.

figure.aria: A block diagram of a unity feedback loop in which the input and the fed-back output meet at the summing node to form the error E of s, which drives G of s.

chapters.example: A unity feedback system has G(s) = 100/[s(s + 10)]. Find the steady-state error for a unit step, a unit ramp and a unit parabola. Answer: one pole at the origin, so type 1. Kp = lim s→0 G(s) = ∞, so the step error is 1/(1 + ∞) = 0. Kv = lim s→0 sG(s) = 100/10 = 10, so the ramp error is 1/10 = 0.1. Ka = lim s→0 s²G(s) = 0, so the parabola error is 1/0 = ∞. The system tracks a step exactly and a ramp with a constant lag.
chapters.trap: Evaluating the constants on the closed-loop transfer function instead of the open-loop one, and quoting a finite error for a system whose closed loop is unstable — the final value theorem then simply does not apply.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.2 for type; Chapter 2.1 for the standard inputs; the final value theorem from Laplace transforms.
chapters.leave: The stability test that must come first to Unit 3; the series form of the error to Chapter 2.7.

chapters.idea: When the input is not a pure step, ramp or parabola, expand E(s)/R(s) about s = 0 into a series and read the dynamic error coefficients C₀, C₁, C₂, … off the terms.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter; keep it short and concrete. Write E(s)/R(s) = 1/(1 + G(s)) and expand it as a Maclaurin series in s about s = 0: E(s)/R(s) = C₀ + C₁s + (C₂/2!)s² + … , with C₀ the value at s = 0, C₁ the first derivative at s = 0, C₂ the second derivative at s = 0, and so on. Transforming term by term gives the generalized error series e(t) = C₀r(t) + C₁ṙ(t) + (C₂/2!)r̈(t) + … . Link the coefficients to Chapter 2.6: C₀ = 1/(1 + Kp), and for a type 1 system C₀ = 0 and C₁ = 1/Kv, so the static constants are the first two terms of this series. Explain that this is what makes the method useful: any slowly varying input can be handled once the coefficients are known. Show the recipe: form E/R, expand by long division or by the binomial expansion, identify the coefficients, apply to the given r(t).

figure.title: From transfer function to error series
figure.aria: A flowchart that expands the ratio E of s over R of s into a Maclaurin series about zero and turns its coefficients into a time-domain error series.

chapters.example: A unity feedback system has G(s) = 10/[s(1 + 0.5s)]. Find C₀, C₁, C₂ and the steady-state error for r(t) = 2 + 4t. Answer: E/R = 1/(1 + G) = s(1 + 0.5s)/[10 + s + 0.5s²]. Put u = (s + 0.5s²)/10, so E/R = u/(1 + u) ≈ u − u² = 0.1s + 0.05s² − 0.01s² = 0.1s + 0.04s². Therefore C₀ = 0, C₁ = 0.1, and C₂/2! = 0.04 so C₂ = 0.08. For r = 2 + 4t we have ṙ = 4 and r̈ = 0, giving ess = C₀r + C₁ṙ = 0 + 0.1 × 4 = 0.4, which agrees with the static result 4/Kv = 4/10.
chapters.trap: The series already contains the factorial, so C₂ is twice the coefficient of s². Also, the series gives a usable steady-state number only if the closed loop is stable and the input derivatives eventually settle.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.6 for Kp, Kv, Ka; Chapter 2.2 for type; Maclaurin expansion from mathematics.
chapters.leave: Stability testing to Unit 3; nonlinear systems, where no such series exists, to Unit 7.
